analysis.one_liner: Requires food delivery apps to show all fees upfront and bar personalized fee formulas.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Commerce Committee since its introduction in April 2026, with no cosponsors and no committee action.
analysis.plain_summary: The PRICE Act would force third-party delivery platforms like DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Grubhub to show the restaurant's own price and any delivery fees on every item, keep a running total of the full order cost on screen, and explain each fee before payment. It also bans fee formulas that secretly vary based on what the platform thinks an individual user is willing to pay, or on backroom terms the platform negotiated with a restaurant. The FTC and state attorneys general would enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: People who order food and goods through delivery apps, who today often see a menu price that differs from the restaurant's in-store price and encounter fees whose size and basis are unclear until checkout. The bill guarantees the in-store price is displayed, fees are itemized and explained, and the running total includes everything before you commit.

how_it_helps.text: Platforms must prominently display the retail establishment's own price for each item (excluding taxes) and any delivery fee the platform adds, whenever the user selects an item.
Throughout the ordering process, the platform must show a running total of everything charged so far, including items, taxes, and fees.
Before asking for payment, the platform must clearly explain each delivery fee, what it is for, the amount, which item it relates to, and whether it is refundable.

Delivery fees must be set by a fixed methodology chosen before the user starts an order, based only on the order price and delivery factors like distance, and may not use proxies for a user's price sensitivity, purchasing history, or willingness to pay, or terms of deals between the platform and the restaurant.
Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, and state attorneys general can sue on behalf of their residents for injunctions, restitution, or damages.

analysis.who_pays: Third-party delivery platforms bear the cost of rebuilding their fee and display systems and lose the ability to charge individually tailored or opaque fees; some of that cost could be passed to customers as higher flat fees, and platforms argue upfront price display can make orders look more expensive and reduce sales.

drawbacks.text: The bill bans fee formulas that rely on a user's prior purchasing behavior or willingness to pay; platforms and some economists argue personalized pricing can lower prices for price-sensitive customers, so a uniform methodology could mean higher fees for some users than under the current system.

Compliance costs for platforms, and the requirement to display the restaurant's in-store price alongside platform fees, may make orders appear costlier and could reduce order volume, which affects restaurants and delivery couriers who depend on that volume.

Fee formulas may not incorporate any factor related to arrangements negotiated between the platform and a restaurant, which limits how platforms can pass along or recover the commissions restaurants pay them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete and ordinary: you see the true, all-in price of your order as you build it, with each fee explained, and fees can't be quietly tailored to what the app thinks you'll tolerate. The costs are real but modest: platforms face compliance work, some customers who benefited from tailored discounts or fees may pay more, and order volumes could dip. On balance this is a straightforward consumer-transparency rule of the kind states and the FTC have separately pursued, with costs concentrated on a few large platforms.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in April 2026, read twice, and referred to the Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors and no further action while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Ben Ray Luján introduced S. 4401, the PRICE Act, on April 27, 2026.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; no further action appears in its history.
Congress remains in session until January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically alive but has made no movement since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no vote and no movement, delivery platforms keep operating under current pricing practices for now; nothing has changed for consumers yet.

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Mexico and the bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PRICE Act and referred it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no opponent has acted on the record; the bill has a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so its partisan shape is unknown.

industries.industry: Third-party delivery platforms (e.g., DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub)
industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to operate a delivery platform without itemized, explained fees, a running all-in price total, and a fixed fee methodology that cannot be tailored to a user's inferred willingness to pay. This directly targets the opaque and personalized fee structures through which these platforms earn money on top of restaurant prices.

The bill requires platforms to display the establishment's own in-store price, which protects restaurants from having their menu prices marked up invisibly. But the ban on fee formulas tied to platform-restaurant arrangements restricts how platforms can account for the commissions restaurants pay, which could shift negotiation dynamics.

analysis.trajectory: A single-sponsor bill with no cosponsors that has sat in committee since April 2026 is unlikely to reach the Senate floor this Congress; the realistic path is that it dies at the end of the session unless Luján attracts cosponsors or the committee schedules a markup.
